title: Elotes Callejeros
subtitle: Mexican street corn with lime mayo, cotija cheese and chilli powder
excerpt: Elotes callejeros are grilled corn cobs slathered in a lime and mayo mixture, rolled in crumbled cheese and dusted with chilli powder. They take 25 minutes and are served on the cob as a snack.
sourceNotes: Elotes callejeros, meaning street corn, are sold by vendors throughout Mexico. The corn is grilled or boiled then coated in a combination of mayo, sour cream, cheese and chilli. In the United States the dish is often called Mexican street corn and has become popular at food markets and restaurants.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes 25 minutes. Each corn cob is grilled until charred in patches, then coated while hot in a mixture of 60g mayonnaise stirred together with 4 tablespoons of sour cream. The cobs are rolled in 100g crumbled cotija or feta cheese and dusted with chilli powder or tajin. Fresh coriander and a squeeze of lime finish each one.

A griddle pan on a high hob works well here and gives good char marks. You can also grill the corn under the oven grill or cook it directly over a gas flame, turning with tongs. The corn is ready when it is bright yellow with dark patches and tender all the way through when pierced. Do not rush this step. Pale, barely coloured corn will taste steamed, not grilled.

items.prepNote: 1 for the mayo mix, 1 for finishing

content.text: Stir together 60g mayonnaise, 4 tablespoons of sour cream and the juice of 1 lime in a small bowl. Add the finely chopped jalapeño if using. Set aside.
Spread 100g crumbled cotija or feta onto a large flat plate. Have the chilli powder or tajin and a bunch of fresh coriander ready near the hob.

Brush 4 ears of corn with the vegetable oil. Heat a griddle pan over a high hob until smoking hot. Place the corn in the pan and cook for 12 to 15 minutes total, turning every 3 to 4 minutes. The corn should have dark char marks and feel tender when pierced with a knife.
While each cob is still hot, spread the mayo mixture over it generously with a spoon or pastry brush. Cover the whole surface.
Roll the coated cob over the crumbled cheese on the plate, pressing gently so the cheese sticks to the mayo. Dust with chilli powder or tajin.
Scatter fresh coriander leaves over each cob and squeeze the second lime over all four. Serve immediately while still hot.

attrs.symptom: The cheese does not stick to the corn
attrs.cause: The mayo mixture was not spread thickly enough, or the corn had cooled before coating
attrs.fix: Apply the mayo mixture while the corn is still very hot. The heat keeps the coating sticky. Use a generous, even layer across the whole cob. Press the cheese firmly into the coating with your hand rather than just rolling.

attrs.symptom: The corn is pale with no char marks despite a long cooking time
attrs.cause: The griddle pan was not hot enough before the corn went in
attrs.fix: Preheat the griddle pan for at least 3 to 4 minutes over a high hob until it begins to smoke. Do not add the corn to a cold or warm pan. The direct contact with a very hot surface is what creates the char.

attrs.symptom: The corn tastes dry and tough rather than juicy and tender
attrs.cause: The corn was overcooked or was not fresh
attrs.fix: Fresh corn in season needs only 12 to 15 minutes on a hot griddle. If the corn looks dull or the husks are dry, blanch the cobs in boiling water for 3 minutes before grilling to rehydrate them slightly.

content.text: Elotes are sold by street vendors all over Mexico, particularly in the evenings. You buy them from a cart and eat them on the spot. The combination of corn, cheese, chilli and lime is one of the most recognisable flavour profiles in Mexican street food. The dish has spread worldwide and appears at food festivals, markets and barbecues far beyond Mexico.
